title: A Confirmatory Paired Evaluation of Generate→Verify→Repair vs LLM‑Only NetOps Suggestions: A Null Result on a Deterministic Synthetic Task Pool
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop) that measured the marginal effect of inserting a deterministic verifier+repair layer (G→V→R) versus accepting an LLM suggestion directly for intent→configuration NetOps tasks. Using a deterministic task generator and a deterministic validator, we sampled K=200 paired tasks, produced one shared generator output per task with gpt-5-mini, and scored both arms against the same validator. Observed outcome: baseline = 200/200 validator‑compliant applies, guarded = 200/200; paired difference = 0.00; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; paired bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) 95% CI = [0.00,0.00]. The repair pathway was never invoked (repair_applied = 0 across all pairs). We release the full preregistration (SHA‑256 a6d73a5c...), execution manifests, per‑episode model/provider traces, and validator traces so others can replay and extend the design. We interpret the null result as a ceiling effect under the chosen task/model/validator conditions and discuss implications for future designs that seek to demonstrate practical verifier/repair utility.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation is a central engineering goal for modern NetOps and AIOps. Generative language models can synthesize device‑level changes from operator intent, but stochastic generation risks proposing regressions or unsafe changes. A common operational architecture therefore inserts a deterministic verifier (emulator/validator) and optional repair stage between suggestion and apply: generate→verify→repair (G→V→R). While prior work and benchmarks argue for the operational value of verification and iterative repair, rigorous quantification of the verifier’s marginal contribution requires preregistered experimental control over generator outputs, verification semantics, and task selection. Without such control, post‑hoc sampling or selective reporting can confound conclusions.
This paper reports a fully preregistered, artifact‑grounded paired evaluation (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop) that isolates the marginal effect of a verifier+repair layer when the generator output is held fixed. Key design decisions were frozen in machine‑readable preregistration (SHA‑256 a6d73a5cc0bda22e691a3634068a881b36ae274a65ab33919a647ec32c56e622) and all artifacts were archived and hashed. Our confirmatory estimand was the paired difference in regression‑causing change rate (guarded − baseline). We used a single shared generation per task with requested_model = gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256: 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa). Across K=200 deterministically sampled tasks (see execution/task_manifest.jsonl SHA‑256 f1d447b7...), both arms returned validator‑compliant applies in every case (n11=200; n10=n01=n00=0), producing a null paired difference. We document the run, present exact inferential results, explain the ceiling effect, and discuss experimental design lessons for future verifier evaluations.
sections.related_work: Two broad research strands motivate our study. First, work that uses LLMs for configuration synthesis, intent translation, and agentic NetOps highlights both promise and risk: generator fluency does not guarantee operational correctness, and hallucinated or incomplete proposals can introduce outages. Representative surveys and position papers argue that LLM outputs must be bounded by formal checks, solver‑backed reasoning, or verifier artifacts to be trustworthy in operations (see recent NetOps/AIOps surveys and Cornetto-style evaluations in the manuscript evidence bundle). Second, the generate→validate→repair pipeline has been advocated and benchmarked (e.g., repair‑focused benchmarks and generate‑validate pipelines) demonstrating that verification can reduce regressions when generators frequently err or when validators detect meaningful faults. Our work differs by preregistering a paired design that holds generator output constant and measures only the marginal verifier/repair effect under deterministic validator semantics. This isolates verifier impact from generator variability and aligns with calls for workflow‑centred evaluation in agentic NetOps literature. The evidence corpus used to assemble our tasks and to position the contribution is archived in the execution bundle and includes recent generate‑validate‑repair and verifier evolution works.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and hypothesis. The full preregistration (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop; SHA‑256 a6d73a5c...) froze the primary estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline), sampling rules, inclusion/exclusion filters, execution budget, and analysis script (paired_binary_analysis_v1). Confirmatory H1 posited that a G→V→R pipeline would yield a lower regression‑causing change rate than the LLM‑only baseline. The power plan assumed a baseline regression rate ≈0.20 and targeted an absolute reduction of 0.08 with alpha=0.05 and power=0.80; sensitivity scans were preregistered.
Paired shared‑generation design. For each intent we generated a single candidate configuration (shared_initial_generation) using the requested model and prompt family. The two experimental arms then used the identical candidate: (1) baseline — accept LLM suggestion and score it; (2) guarded — run deterministic validator on the candidate and, if validator fails, optionally invoke one automated repair call (maximum_repair_calls_per_task=1). This design isolates the verifier’s marginal effect by removing generator variability. The deterministic task generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) and deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) were preregistered; task generation seeds and manifest entries are archived (execution/task_manifest.jsonl SHA‑256 f1d447b7...).
Task sampling and inclusion. Tasks were deterministically assembled from the synthetic pool and filtered to those covered by validator semantics. The sampling procedure was: compute SHA‑256(intent_string), sort ascending, select first K=200 tasks. Automated exclusion rules (validator coverage failures, duplicate hashes) were enforced and logged; no human selection occurred post‑lock. Task payloads encode explicit workflow constraints (e.g., make‑before‑break, shut‑then‑change MTU) and expected final_state snapshots to make scoring objective; examples appear in the representative task manifest entries archived under execution/ (see execution/responses and execution/scoring paths).
Validator semantics and scoring. The validator parses configuration lines into structured operations, applies preregistered dependency rules (e.g., interfaces requiring admin down for MTU or VLAN changes, final‑group minima), and produces a binary valid flag plus structured diagnostics (parsed_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, normalized_configuration, final_state snapshot). The scoring rule for the primary outcome was full_intent_constraint_validation (execution/scoring/*.json). If guarded validation failed, the preregistered repair policy allowed one constrained repair call; repaired candidates would be revalidated once. All validator traces and decision reasons were recorded to support traceable audit.
Execution logging, provenance, and reproducibility. The run used adapter_family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1 and provider = openai_responses; all provider calls, raw responses, and validator traces were persisted and hashed. Key artifact hashes: raw_results.jsonl (execution/raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 3dfbe1b6580c9df4233332164d0453e2aecdb34d52a01883358d67ac30e028e6), model_configuration.json (SHA‑256 1acce92558edeb13cd97...), transformation_manifest.json (SHA‑256 79c91155...), and master prompt provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256 1872df1e...). The execution manifest records model_calls_used=200 and completed_episode_count=400 (two arms × 200 tasks). Per‑call provider audit logs and call_cache entries were stored to detect caching or stateful anomalies. Analysis code and parameters (bootstrap seed 1729, resamples 10000) are archived (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl).
sections.results:
Execution and primary outcome. The autonomous run completed as preregistered: planned episodes = 400, completed episodes = 400, failed episodes = 0, model_calls_used = 200 (one shared generation per task). The sample used for confirmatory inference contained complete_pairs = 200. Validator scoring produced the paired contingency table:
- n11 (guarded=success, baseline=success) = 200
- n10 (guarded=success, baseline=failure) = 0
- n01 (guarded=failure, baseline=success) = 0
- n00 (both failure) = 0
(analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 7bc1bd2a...).
Statistical inference. The preregistered primary estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline) equals 0.00 on the observed data. We conducted the preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test (appropriate for paired binary outcomes) which returned p = 1.00. We computed a paired bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval with 10,000 resamples and seed=1729 (as preregistered); the resulting 95% CI is [0.00, 0.00]. All statistical artifacts and logs are archived under analysis/ (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl SHA‑256 52a0858d...).
Repair pathway and resource accounting. The guarded policy’s repair pathway was never used: repair_applied==false in every execution/scoring JSON trace (example: execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json). Consequently, the verifier did not block or alter any apply and the model call budget was identical to the baseline in practice. Provider audit aggregated hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 (no failed provider calls recorded) and cache_miss_count = 200 (no cache hits). The deterministic reconciliation artifact (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json) confirms episode accounting consistency and that cross‑condition cache reuse did not occur.
Representative diagnostics. Representative scoring JSONs contain normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, and final_state snapshots to support external replay. Representative examples (execution/responses/task-000001-*.txt and execution/scoring/task-000001-*.json) show canonical MTU and VLAN migration intents where the LLM candidate satisfied workflow constraints and the validator flagged zero violations. The full response and scoring bundles are hashed and archived for independent verification.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation: ceiling effect and bounded scope. The observed degenerate null (100% success in both arms) reflects a ceiling effect under the chosen combination of (i) deterministic synthetic task pool filtered to validator coverage, (ii) a capable generator under the shared generation prompt family (requested_model gpt-5-mini), and (iii) a deterministic validator whose coverage matched the sampled intents. Under those conditions, the verifier had no opportunity to intervene: generator outputs already satisfied the verifier constraints and no repairs were needed. This is an internally valid result for the preregistered estimand but it does not imply verifiers are unnecessary in general; instead it indicates that to demonstrate marginal verifier value the evaluation must select task/model regimes with nontrivial baseline error rates or use adversarial/near‑coverage tasks.
Design lessons for future confirmatory studies. We highlight three reproducible paths forward (all consistent with our artifacts and preregistration): (1) increase baseline error propensity by sampling intents outside or at the edge of validator coverage (the preregistered sampling and exclusion logs permit deterministic expansion of the pool); (2) evaluate across multiple generator strengths or deliberately degrade generator capability to create measurable failure modes; (3) adopt an interactive generator–verifier protocol where the generator can react to verifier feedback (changes the estimand but better matches agentic operational workflows). Each path trades internal isolation for operational realism; preregistration of the chosen trade‑offs is crucial to avoid researcher degrees of freedom.
Threats to validity and mitigations. Internal validity: maintained by deterministic sampling, frozen seeds, and archived hashes—every key artifact (master prompt, model config, raw responses, scoring traces) is available for replay. Construct validity: our primary outcome measured validator.valid; its operational meaning depends on validator fidelity. External validity: the experiment used a single requested_model (gpt-5-mini) and synthetic tasks; generalizing to production intents, other models, or imperfect validators is not supported by the observed data. Conclusion validity: preregistered power calculations assumed a nontrivial baseline error rate; the observed baseline=1.0 violated that assumption and therefore the null cannot be taken as evidence of absence of verifier benefit outside the sampled regime. All these points and artifact locations are documented in the reproducibility bundle to allow others to modify sampling or generator settings and rerun confirmatory variants.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory comparison of G→V→R versus an LLM‑only suggestion pipeline, archiving all artifacts and hashes. Under the deterministic synthetic task pool and deterministic validator that we sampled, the generator proposals satisfied validation in every task and the guarded verifier+repair stage never invoked a repair (repair_applied = 0), producing a null paired difference (0.00) with exact McNemar p = 1.00 and bootstrap 95% CI [0.00,0.00]. This result documents a ceiling case and demonstrates the practical necessity of designing failure‑rich evaluations (or interacting generator–verifier protocols) when the research objective is to quantify verifier or automated repair utility. We release the complete preregistration, execution manifest, per‑call provider traces, response artifacts, and analysis scripts to enable exact replay and to support future preregistered studies that vary task selection, generator capabilities, and verifier coverage to produce interpretable, operationally meaningful estimates of verifier value. All archived artifacts are referenced below and in the Disclosure Statement for independent verification.

limitations: Single requested_model (gpt-5-mini) evaluated—results do not generalize to other LLMs without additional experiments.
Synthetic deterministic task pool filtered to validator coverage—external validity to production change intents and natural operator distributions is limited.
Primary outcome measures validator.valid; construct validity depends on validator fidelity and on whether validator behavior matches real devices and control‑plane dynamics.
Ceiling effect (baseline success = 100%) invalidates the preregistered power assumption and prevents demonstration of verifier/repair benefit under these conditions.
Residual contamination (undetectable pretraining overlap) cannot be fully excluded despite hashing and logging; contamination_summary.csv recorded no flagged items for this run.
